A1.justification: Both PDFs are complete, readable 24-page versions of the same NeuSA paper. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison, including matching retained content across renumbering and relocation.

before.justification: v1 reports original numerical experiments on wave, sine-Gordon, and Burgers equations, including temporal extrapolation, a four-layer wave case, and repeated-run results in Appendix C.

after.justification: v2 retains original PDE-solving experiments and adds Marmousi and 3D wave evaluations, a frequency sensitivity experiment, and inference-time measurements.

M1.justification: v1 explicitly learns the spectral basis through trainable orthogonal transformations, described in Section 2.1 and Appendix B.1.1. v2 removes this component throughout the proposed procedure. This drops a featured architectural capability, although spectral projection, NODE evolution, analytical initialization, dimension-wise layers, and physics-informed losses remain.

E1.justification: v2 adds wave propagation in the complex 2D Marmousi medium and a two-layer 3D medium, plus 1D Burgers for frequency sensitivity. It removes v1's additional four-layer 2D wave case. The original three-layer 2D wave, 1D sine-Gordon, and 2D Burgers tasks remain.

E2.justification: Corresponding retained experiments still compare PINN, QRes, FLS, and PINNsFormer. New Marmousi and 3D tests use PINN, QRes, and FLS, while the inference comparison reuses the existing architectures. Newly cited neural spectral and operator-learning methods are not evaluated as new baselines.

E3.justification: Section 3.3 changes NeuSA's stated Burgers integration from 101 to 201 time steps and revises the second initial-condition component from cos(pi*x2)^2 to cos(pi*x1)cos(pi*x2). Appendix D introduces a 61–141-frequency sweep and uniform-grid inference timing with specified grid sizes. These are reported setting and evaluation-design changes; the PDFs do not establish which existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New Appendix D examines frequency count versus accuracy and training cost, and compares inference costs across three tasks. The Burgers extrapolation curves and snapshots are revised. Conversely, v1's four-layer wave stress case, its discussion of thin-layer difficulties, and associated training-loss analysis are removed.

E5.justification: Appendix C.4 retains seven seeds for the 2D experiments, three for sine-Gordon, and reporting of means and standard deviations. New benchmark tables extend this reporting practice without introducing a new uncertainty procedure or an explicit increase in runs. The new 3D experiment's run count is unspecified.

E6.justification: v2 adds Marmousi, 3D wave, frequency-sensitivity, and inference-time results, and replaces the Burgers extrapolation plots. Table 1 changes NeuSA's Burgers rMSE/training time from 0.115/62 seconds to 0.051/112 seconds, reversing its accuracy ranking against QRes under revised stated settings. However, v2 Table 6 retains 0.115/62 seconds, leaving an unresolved inconsistency. The four-layer wave results are removed.

T1.justification: v1's explicit learned-basis projection and reconstruction definitions in Appendix B.1.1, Equation 21, are removed. The causality assumptions, Theorems 1 and 2 and their proof, spectral derivative derivations, and Runge–Kutta stability argument otherwise remain substantively unchanged.

C1.justification: The introduction withdraws the claim that NeuSA is the first spectral-method-based architecture for neural PDEs and removes the entire 'Learnable representations' contribution. This materially narrows the claimed novelty and capabilities. The principal causality, spectral fidelity, analytical initialization, and temporal extrapolation claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations of the frequency–stability–runtime tradeoff and attributes large-grid baseline inference costs to possible memory swapping. It removes the specific thin-layer failure discussion and changes the Burgers interpretation from competitive with QRes to outperforming it. Existing geometry, stiffness, and initialization limitations remain in the relocated limitations appendix.

D1.justification: v2 replaces the future code-release promise with a statement that code and pretrained models are available, supplying a repository link. It removes the explicit three-layer velocity formula from v1 Appendix C.1 and the orthogonal-map implementation details. Hardware, library versions, and most solver and sampling disclosures remain. Repository availability was not independently checked.

R1.justification: v2 substantially revises novelty positioning by acknowledging Du et al.'s Neural spectral methods where v1 claimed precedence. It also adds spectral operator learning, Flowing, a flow-structured networks thesis, and the Marmousi reference, while removing the orthogonal-parametrization reference. The important change is recognition of directly related spectral neural work, beyond bibliography renumbering.

P1.justification: There is extensive paragraph-level rewriting across the introduction, related work, method explanation, and experimental narrative, alongside a revised contribution list. v2 adds an Additional experiments appendix, moves Limitations from D to E, and adds acknowledgments. Author names, affiliations, and conference-header information are also revised.

P2.justification: Table 1 is redesigned from three tasks with rMAE/rMSE/time to five with rMSE/time; rMAE remains in appendix tables. v2 adds Marmousi and 3D figures and four tables, redraws the extrapolation display, and removes the four-layer wave and training-domain Burgers figures. Existing architecture diagrams and sine-Gordon results are retained across renumbering.

improvement.justification: The realistic Marmousi and 3D tests, computational-cost analyses, more qualified novelty positioning, and code-access statement strengthen the paper. However, v2 introduces conflicting Burgers results: Table 1 reports 0.051 rMSE and 112 seconds, while Table 6 retains v1's 0.115 and 62 seconds, changing whether NeuSA beats QRes. It also removes the earlier four-layer failure analysis. These benefits and unresolved losses in reporting consistency and failure characterization prevent a reliable net-quality judgment.
